title: Craniofacial syndromes
description: Congenital and developmental syndromes affecting the face, jaws, palate, and dentition — most are referred to specialist multidisciplinary care, but the GDP is often first to notice.

problems.description: Child born with split in the lip and roof of the mouth, struggling to feed, with impaired hearing and speech.
problems.etiology: Multifactorial — both genetic and environmental factors drive it. On the environmental side: maternal smoking, alcohol use, and phenytoin intake all increase risk [1]. The genetic contribution is real too — family history shows up in 40% of combined cleft lip and palate cases, and in about 20% of isolated cleft palate [2]. So it can run as an isolated anomaly or as part of a wider syndrome [1]. The takeaway: always ask about family history and maternal drug exposure.
problems.presentation: The cleft itself can sit anywhere on a spectrum: lip only, palate only, or both; unilateral or bilateral; complete or incomplete [3]. What you can miss is the submucous cleft — the overlying mucosa is intact, so it looks fine until someone flags the child's speech [3]. Beyond the visible cleft, look for the associated package: impaired hearing, disordered speech, hypodontia and displaced teeth near the cleft site, hypoplastic and delayed-erupting teeth [4]. And in up to 20% of cases, congenital anomalies elsewhere.
problems.results: The tissue deficit, displaced alveolar segments, and abnormal muscle attachments are the structural problem [5]. What happens is that primary surgical repair — the very thing that fixes the cleft — also restrains maxillary growth. Repaired clefts show reduced growth in all three dimensions: anteroposterior, transverse, and vertical [6]. The practical consequence is a Class III malocclusion in adolescence, baked in by the surgery itself [7].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Orofacial cleft — with or without alveolar involvement — plus hearing impairment and disordered speech. Hypodontia and displaced teeth at the cleft site are characteristic dental findings [4]. One useful prevention fact: folic acid at the start of pregnancy cuts the risk fourfold [8]. Worth sharing with families at any point in early dental contact.
problems.treatment: This is MDT territory. Refer to the specialist cleft team — cleft surgeon, ENT surgeon, orthodontist, speech therapist, and clinical psychologist [9]. Your role as the GDP is establishing good preventive dental care early and supporting the family through a long journey. Know the surgical staging: lip closure at 3–6 months, palatal closure at 9–12 months, then alveolar bone graft when the canine root is half to two-thirds formed — roughly 8½ to 10½ years [10]. Centralised care with outcome audit gives meaningfully better results [9].
problems.prognosis: Coordinated MDT management has substantially improved speech, occlusion, and facial appearance over time. But the growth restriction from primary surgery is an inherent trade-off — some patients end up with skeletal discrepancy too severe for conventional osteotomy and need distraction osteogenesis [11]. The nasal deformity remains the hardest surgical problem to solve [12].

citations.quote: Multifactorial with both genetic and environmental factors (including maternal smoking, alcohol, and phenytoin intake) involved.
CLP varies with racial group and geographically. Occurs in ~1:1000 Caucasian births, but prevalence i. M > F. If unilateral L > R. Family history in 40% of cases.

Many exist, but the best approach is to describe cleft: 1° &/or 2° palate; complete or incomplete; unilateral or bilateral. Submucous cleft of the palate is often missed until poor speech noticed, as overlying mucosa is intact.
In CLP, ↑ prevalence of hypodontia and $ teeth (especially in region of cleft). Teeth adjacent to cleft are often displaced. Also ↑ incidence of hypoplasia and delayed eruption.
Tissue deficit, displacement of segments, and abnormal muscle attachments.
Unrepaired clefts show normal growth. In repaired clefts maxillary growth is ↓ AP, transversely, and vertically. Mandibular growth also d.
Because of the restraining effects of 1° surgery upon facial growth, cleft patients often have a Class III malocclusion.
Taking folic acid at the start of pregnancy reduces the risk of cleft lip and palate fourfold.

Team usually includes cleft surgeon, ear, nose, and throat (ENT) surgeon, health visitors, orthodontist, speech therapist, clinical psychologist, and central coordinator. Centralization of care and audit of outcome gives better results.
If an alveolar cleft is present then this should be grafted when the canine root is half to two-thirds formed (around age 8½ to 10½yrs) with cancellous bone.
A proportion of cleft patients will have a skeletal discrepancy that is too severe for conventional surgical movements.
Perhaps the greatest surgical challenge. 1° functional lip/nose repair may alter this.

problems.description: Patient with characteristic flat mid-face, large tongue, and delayed tooth eruption, known to have a heart condition and neck instability risk.
problems.etiology: The commonest of all malformation syndromes — up to 1:600 births — and the risk climbs with maternal age [1]. The cause is chromosomal: trisomy 21. That's the whole story on aetiology. What matters clinically is understanding the associated conditions, because they directly shape how you deliver dental care.
problems.presentation: The facial picture is recognisable: brachycephaly, mid-face retrusion, flattened nasal bridge, upward-sloping palpebral fissures [1]. Intra-orally, relative macroglossia and delayed tooth eruption are consistent findings [1]. Now, the associations you need to hold in mind for dental care: cardiac defects, atlanto-axial subluxation risk, anaemia, and an increased leukaemia risk [1]. Most patients are extremely cooperative — don't let the diagnosis lower your ambition for their dental care [1].
problems.results: Children with Down syndrome make up about a third of severely mentally handicapped children [1]. The atlanto-axial subluxation risk is the one that changes what you do in the chair — any position that hyperextends the neck puts the cord at risk. So chair positioning and any procedure requiring neck movement need adjusting. Periodontal disease also tends to be more severe than you'd expect for the level of plaque.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Macroglossia, delayed eruption, and mid-face retrusion in the context of trisomy 21 [1]. The combination of cardiac defects and atlanto-axial subluxation risk isn't incidental — it directly shapes anaesthetic and chair-side risk. Worth knowing these before the appointment, not discovering them during.
problems.treatment: You can and should provide routine dental care — but with adjustments. Check for cardiac defects and apply antibiotic prophylaxis where indicated. Position the neck carefully throughout treatment to avoid atlanto-axial stress. Adapt your communication style: simple language, shorter appointments, familiar environment. Refer to specialist services for complex restorative or surgical work. Management is lifelong and supportive.
problems.prognosis: Life expectancy has increased significantly with improved cardiac and medical management. The main dental concern long-term is periodontal disease — monitor proactively and don't underestimate it. Most patients engage well with primary dental care when you get the environment right.

citations.quote: The commonest of all malformation syndromes, affecting up to 1:600 births. Risk ↑ with maternal age. Children with Down syndrome account for one-third of severely mentally handicapped children. Facial appearance is characteristic with brachycephaly, mid-face retrusion, small nose with flattened nasal bridge, and upward sloping palpebral fissures (formerly known as 'mongoloid slant'). There is relative macroglossia and delayed eruption of teeth. Major relevant associations are heart defects, atlanto-axial subluxation, anaemia, and an ↑ risk of leukaemia. Most children and adults with Down syndrome are extremely friendly and cooperative.

problems.description: Patient with very small lower jaw, flat cheekbones, downward-slanting eyes, and deformed ears — deaf, but with fully normal intellect.
problems.etiology: The reason is that the first branchial arch doesn't develop properly — so everything derived from it is affected [1]. It's autosomal dominant with variable expressivity, which means you can see the full picture in one family member and a subtle version in another [1].
problems.presentation: The facial picture here is striking. Downward-sloping palpebral fissures, flat malar complexes, mandibular retrognathia with a high gonial angle, deformed pinnae [1]. Middle and inner ear hypoplasia causes deafness — conductive deafness, not neural [1]. About 30% have a cleft palate, and 25% have an unusual hair projection pointing towards the cheek [1]. The thing is, intellectual function is completely normal in most patients [1] — but deafness and unusual facial appearance lead to their potential being badly underestimated.
problems.results: Normal intellect is the key finding here, and it's easily missed [1]. The degree of mandibular and malar hypoplasia determines how much surgical work is needed. Deafness — if unidentified and untreated early — shapes educational and social outcomes more than the facial appearance does. So the question is: has the hearing been properly assessed?
problems.definingCharacteristics: Mandibular retrognathia, malar hypoplasia, downward-slanting eyes, and conductive deafness — with fully intact intellect [1]. That last point matters enormously for how you communicate with and advocate for the patient. This syndrome is described as a prime indication for corrective craniofacial surgery [1].
problems.treatment: Refer to a craniofacial MDT. Your role as the GDP is recognition, appropriate onward referral, and providing routine dental care in the meantime. Craniofacial surgery addresses the skeletal deformity; hearing aids or cochlear implants address the deafness. Repair cleft palate where present via the usual pathway.
problems.prognosis: With craniofacial surgical intervention and early hearing rehabilitation, functional and aesthetic outcomes can improve substantially. The intellectual potential is normal — so outcomes depend heavily on whether the deafness is caught and treated early, and whether professionals see past the facial appearance.

citations.quote: This basically involves defects in structures derived from the first branchial arch. It is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable expressivity, and consists of downward-sloping palpebral fissures (formerly known as 'antimongoloid slant'), hypoplastic malar complexes, mandibular retrognathia with a high gonial angle, deformed pinnas, hypoplastic air sinuses, colobomas in the outer third of the eye, and middle and inner ear hypoplasia (and hence deafness). About 30% have cleft palates and 25% have an unusual tongue-like projection of hair pointing towards the cheek. Most have completely normal intellectual function, which may be missed because they are deaf and 'funny-looking kids'. These people may well miss out on fulfilling their potential because of society's (and some professionals') attitude to deformity. This syndrome is a prime indication for corrective craniofacial surgery.

problems.description: Newborn with very small lower jaw, cleft palate, and tongue falling back, causing airway obstruction and feeding difficulty.
problems.etiology: This is a sequence, not a syndrome — and that distinction matters. The initiating event is micrognathia. The small jaw prevents the tongue from descending, so the tongue sits high and disrupts palatal shelf fusion — producing glossoptosis and cleft palate as downstream consequences [1]. The associated anomaly list is huge [1]. Importantly, about 30% of Robin sequence patients have Stickler syndrome underneath it — a connective tissue disorder bringing flat mid-face, myopia, retinal detachment, hearing loss, and arthropathy [2].
problems.presentation: The triad: micrognathia, cleft palate, glossoptosis [1]. The immediate problem is airway — the tongue falls back and obstructs. In the newborn, this is life-threatening. Associated anomalies are common, so full paediatric assessment is essential. Examine the eyes: Stickler syndrome needs to be actively screened for given how frequently it underlies this sequence [2].
problems.results: Neonatal airway obstruction is the acute risk — it defines the urgency. The cleft palate impairs speech development. When Stickler syndrome is present, add retinal detachment risk and significant hearing loss to the picture [2]. The breadth of associated anomalies means you can't treat this as just a jaw and palate problem.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Micrognathia + cleft palate + glossoptosis — the defining triad [1]. It's a sequence, not a syndrome: micrognathia drives the rest. That's worth understanding because it frames management — fixing the jaw is the upstream intervention. And with 30% of cases linked to Stickler syndrome, eye examination is non-negotiable [2].
problems.treatment: Neonatal airway management is the immediate priority — this is paediatric and craniofacial territory, not GDP territory. Your role is recognition and urgent referral at first presentation. After the airway is secured, subsequent management follows the cleft pathway. Arrange ophthalmic assessment — the 30% Stickler prevalence makes this essential [2].
problems.prognosis: With prompt airway management the immediate crisis is controlled. Mandibular catch-up growth occurs in many cases, reducing the severity of retrognathia over time. Long-term outcomes hinge on the associated anomalies — particularly hearing and vision in those with Stickler syndrome.

citations.quote: Named after Pierre Robin (and mistakenly called Pierre Robin syndrome at times). This is micrognathia, cleft palate, and glossoptosis. Huge number of associated anomalies.

Perhaps the commonest syndrome associated with cleft palate (20%). Consists of flat mid-face, cleft palate, myopia, retinal detachment, hearing loss (80%), and arthropathy. About 30% of Robin sequence patients have Stickler syndrome, therefore examine eyes.

problems.description: Patient with multiple bony lumps on the jaw and face, skin cysts, and a strong family history — incidental finding on dental X-ray.
problems.etiology: Autosomal dominant [1]. The syndrome is a triad: multiple osteomas of the jaws and facial bones, multiple polyps of the large intestine, and epidermoid cysts and fibromas of the skin [1]. The reason it matters to you as a GDP is that the jaw osteomas — which are benign and clinically harmless on their own — are the entry point to a potentially lethal GI diagnosis.
problems.presentation: Multiple osteomas on the jaws and facial bones, often picked up incidentally on a dental panoramic radiograph [1]. Associated epidermoid cysts and fibromas are the cutaneous findings to note [1]. The intestinal polyps are typically asymptomatic at the point of dental presentation — which is exactly why they get missed.
problems.results: The intestinal polyps carry a high risk of malignant transformation [1]. So finding jaw osteomas on clinical examination or X-ray mandates lower GI investigation [1]. Missing this step has serious consequences. The interesting bit is that this is described as a highly 'worthwhile' syndrome — precisely because dental incidental findings can trigger life-saving GI surveillance [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Multiple jaw osteomas + large intestine polyps prone to rapid malignant change + epidermoid skin cysts, inherited as an autosomal dominant [1]. The dental finding is the entry point to diagnosis. Multiple jaw osteomas in a patient with a relevant family history should immediately prompt you to investigate further.
problems.treatment: Recognise the jaw osteomas — clinically and on radiographs — and refer for GI investigation. The osteomas themselves are benign and may not need removal. GI management is the priority: surveillance colonoscopy and polyp removal, handled by gastroenterology and colorectal surgery. Your job is to spot it and escalate.
problems.prognosis: If the intestinal polyps are identified and managed before malignant change, prognosis is good. Untreated, the polyp burden carries a high lifetime risk of colorectal carcinoma. The dental presentation is an important early diagnostic opportunity — it's worth being alert to.

citations.quote: This comprises multiple osteomas (particularly of the jaws and facial bones), multiple polyps of the large intestine, epidermoid cysts, and fibromas of the skin. It shows autosomal dominant inheritance. The discovery on clinical or X-ray examination of facial osteomas mandates examination of the lower gastrointestinal tract, as these polyps have a tendency to rapid malignant change. This is a highly 'worthwhile' syndrome.

problems.description: Patient with multiple skin cancers, multiple jaw cysts on X-ray, prominent forehead, and bifid ribs — several jaw cysts recur after treatment.
problems.conditionName: Gorlin–Goltz syndrome (multiple basal cell naevi syndrome)
problems.etiology: Autosomal dominant [1]. Here's the combination: multiple basal cell carcinomas, multiple odontogenic keratocysts of the jaws, vertebral and rib anomalies (usually bifid ribs), and calcification of the falx cerebri [1]. What makes this syndrome clinically significant for the GDP is that the jaw cysts — often asymptomatic — show up on routine OPG long before the full picture is recognised.
problems.presentation: Multiple BCCs appearing earlier in life than typical BCC presentation [1]. Multiple jaw cysts — odontogenic keratocysts — found incidentally on panoramic radiographs [1]. Frontal bossing, mandibular prognathism, hypertelorism, and calcified falx cerebri on skull imaging [1]. The rule of thumb: multiple jaw cysts in a young patient, or several simultaneous jaw cysts at any age, should make you think of this syndrome.
problems.results: Odontogenic keratocysts in Gorlin–Goltz have a high recurrence rate after removal — they need long-term follow-up [1]. The BCCs require ongoing dermatological surveillance. Hydrocephalus and eye and endocrine abnormalities have also been reported [1]. So this is a multi-system condition that needs coordinated specialist oversight, not just jaw surgery.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Multiple odontogenic keratocysts of the jaws + multiple BCCs + bifid ribs + calcified falx cerebri, with frontal bossing and mandibular prognathism [1]. A young patient with several jaw cysts on OPG is the classic dental presentation. The recurrence of the cysts after treatment is a further clue — ordinary keratocysts recur, but not like this.
problems.treatment: Recognise the pattern — multiple or recurrent jaw cysts on radiographs — and refer to oral and maxillofacial surgery and dermatology. The OMFS team manage the jaw cysts (enucleation with or without peripheral ostectomy; Carnoy's solution is used in some centres). Dermatology handles BCC surveillance. Arrange genetic counselling given the autosomal dominant inheritance.
problems.prognosis: BCCs in this syndrome are locally destructive but rarely metastasise. The jaw cysts recur frequently and need lifelong radiographic surveillance. Overall prognosis depends on the BCC burden and whether the diagnosis is made early enough to drive proactive management — which is why the OPG incidental finding matters so much.

citations.quote: Consists of multiple BCCs (epitheliomas), multiple jaw cysts (odontogenic keratocysts), vertebral and rib anomalies (usually bifid ribs), and calcification of the falx cerebri. Frontal bossing, mandibular prognathism, hypertelorism, hydrocephalus, and eye and endocrine abnormalities have also been noted.
